content: Your doctor has prescribed sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, a combination antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication will be administered intravenously, meaning it will be added to a fluid that drips into your vein through a needle or catheter. The infusion typically lasts 60 to 90 minutes or longer and is given two to four times daily. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim work together to eliminate bacteria responsible for various infections, including pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and intestinal infections. In some cases, this medication may be used for other purposes; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and any potential side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is essential to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to sulfamethoxazole, trimethoprim, other sulfa drugs, diuretics (commonly referred to as water pills), oral diabetes medications, or any other drugs. Additionally, provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, especially anticoagulants (such as warfarin), cyclosporine, diabetes medications, diuretics, seizure medications (such as phenytoin), methotrexate, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of alcoholism or if you have or have ever had liver or kidney disease, asthma, severe allergies, anemia, or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G-6-PD) deficiency, which is an inherited blood disorder. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking this medication, contact your doctor immediately. Before administering the medication, inspect the solution carefully. It should appear clear and free of any floating particles. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. If you encounter any of these issues, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is crucial to follow your healthcare provider's instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop the treatment on your own, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you experience a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim may cause side effects. Minor side effects include dizziness or loss of balance, loss of appetite, and an upset stomach. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your healthcare provider. Severe side effects require immediate medical attention. These include a sore throat, difficulty breathing, fever, headache, joint or muscle pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, swelling of the lips or tongue, difficulty swallowing, skin rash or changes, fatigue, unusual bleeding or bruising, weakness, paleness, cough, or diarrhea. If you experience any severe side effects, you or your doctor may report them to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Your healthcare provider will likely teach you how to prepare each dose of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim. Since the medication is only stable for a limited time after preparation, it is important to prepare your daily doses as instructed. Your healthcare provider will also provide instructions on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim intravenously, it is important to recognize the signs of a catheter-related infection, which can occur at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin. Symptoms of such an infection include tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, and pain. If you notice any of these symptoms, inform your healthcare provider immediately. This medication is available under the brand names Bactrim Injection® and Septra Injection®, as well as generic names such as Sulfamethoxazole and Trimethoprim Injection, SMX-TMP Injection, and TMP-SMX Injection.
